label: Institution
name: Aghlabids
summary:
The Aghlabid dynasty (800–909 CE) was an Arab dynasty that governed Ifriqiya (modern Tunisia and eastern Algeria) as nominal vassals of the Abbasid Caliphate. Under Aghlabid rule, North Africa experienced a renaissance in architecture, learning, and Islamic culture, while Aghlabid fleets transformed the central Mediterranean and conquered Sicily.

Ibrahim I ibn al-Aghlab founded the dynasty with considerable autonomy from Baghdad, building a powerful Mediterranean fleet that conquered Sicily in 827 CE — a campaign that began with 10,000 troops under Asad ibn al-Furat and concluded 75 years later with the complete Islamization of the island. Sicily under Arab rule became a center of advanced agriculture (introducing cotton, citrus fruits, and sugar cane to Europe), astronomy, and medicine that profoundly influenced later Norman Sicily.

The Aghlabid capital Kairouan became one of the holiest cities in Islam and a center of Islamic learning. The Great Mosque of Kairouan, greatly expanded by the Aghlabids, is among the oldest mosques in the western Islamic world. The dynasty fell to the Fatimid invasion of 909 CE, which replaced Sunni Aghlabid rule with Ismaili Shia governance.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Aghlabid conquest of Sicily created a channel through which Islamic agricultural, scientific, and architectural innovations reached medieval Europe during a crucial developmental period.
